reason: I want to start the circulation loop by letting seawater enter seafloor fractures.
expectation: I expect mineral-bearing seawater to move into the fractures, though I’m unsure how it differs from using the early sea.

alternatives.reason: The accumulating sea could also supply water to the fractures, but I chose the mineral-bearing sea.

effect: Seawater has entered the crust, so the next step is to follow it toward hot rock.
reaction: The circulation loop is beginning in a straightforward way.
reason: The only offered combination should heat the infiltrating seawater.
expectation: I expect the seawater to heat up and possibly react with the rock.

effect: The water is heated under pressure; I’ll follow its continued interaction with the rock.
reaction: The pressure explanation clarifies how the fluid stays beneath the surface.
reason: This is the only offered combination and may advance the circulation loop.
expectation: I expect further water–rock reactions, possibly releasing dissolved minerals.

effect: The heated water has exchanged dissolved material with the rock; I’ll follow the fluid back through the fractures.
reaction: The dependence on rock, pressure and temperature makes the reaction more informative.
reason: The only offered combination may return the hydrothermal fluid to the sea.
expectation: I expect the mineral-bearing fluid to rise through the fractures, possibly emerging at a vent.

effect: The fluid is rising through a separate return route, driven by buoyancy and pressure differences.
reaction: The explanation makes the circulation loop clearer.
reason: Mixing the returning fluid with cooler seawater may form the vent deposit.
expectation: I expect the fluid to emerge and cool, possibly precipitating dissolved minerals.

alternatives.reason: Returning the fluid to the early sea also fits the circulation goal, but cooling seems more directly relevant to the deposit.

effect: Cooling and mixing have precipitated minerals; I’ll use them to build the vent deposit.
reaction: It is satisfying to see dissolved material become solid as the fluid cools.
reason: Combining the precipitating minerals with the fractures seems likely to build the deposit around the vent.
expectation: I expect a mineral deposit to form around the vent opening.

alternatives.reason: Returning the hot fluid to the sea addresses the other goal, but I’ll finish the deposit first.

effect: The vent deposit is complete; returning the heated fluid to the sea remains.
reaction: The modest deposit is a useful contrast to assuming every vent builds a tall chimney.
reason: The only offered combination addresses the remaining circulation goal.
expectation: I expect the hot fluid to return to the sea, completing the circulation loop.

effect: The hot fluid returned to the sea as a plume, completing the circulation goal; its visible material is suspended mineral particles, not smoke.
reaction: The distinction between the plume and smoke was a useful final clarification.

mostWorthwhile.text: Cooling the hydrothermal fluid to precipitate minerals was most worthwhile: it connected dissolved material, mixing and the formation of a solid deposit.

leastWorthwhile.text: Heating the water and then combining it with hot rock again felt a little repetitive, although the second step explained the chemical exchange.

surprise.text: The vent deposit was modest rather than necessarily a towering chimney, and the plume was suspended mineral material rather than smoke.

arbitrary.text: The initial choice between two seawater sources had no clear distinction in purpose from the information available.

continue.text: I would continue: the circulation loop gave a clear, useful account of how heat and water move minerals through rock, though the largely sequential choices offered limited decision-making.
